transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-09 15:00 UTC
Duration: 1h15m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Evan Morales (Rift Head of Platform), Priya Singh (Rift SRE), Jared Holt (Rift ML)

Summary:
Quick lat-deep dive on root causes of p95/p99 spikes: interconnect hops, KV serialization overhead, and differences between streaming vs non-streaming token paths. Agreed to run targeted microbenchmarks and share traces.

Topics:
- network hops & MTU/TCP effects
- K-V cache serialization and hotkey sharding
- streaming vs non-streaming tail behavior
- batching strategies and quantization tradeoffs
- VPC peering / TLS / keepalives

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: ok, thanks everyone for taking time. quick context, Rift reported intermittent p99 jumps when traffic goes over their cross-region interconnect, and some requests that use a dense KV lookup set are seeing long tail. we want to triage root cause and propose mitigations.
[00:22] Evan Morales: yeah, we saw like normal p50s ~60ms but p99s spike to 1.2s. happens more during bursts or when we hit certain document ids.
[00:35] Priya Singh: and note, we run across a transit VPC link that hits a firewall appliance, so there are extra hops. also MTU is default 1500.
[00:47] Liam O'Connor: that could be a contributor—extra hops plus TLS handshakes for short-lived connections amplify tail. Also curious about the KV serialization step: are you serializing full protobuf per-key or batching them?
[01:05] Jared Holt: right now it's per-key protobuf, sync call per token when we miss cache. it's simpler but i suspect too chatty.
[01:17] Maya Chen: ok that aligns with a typical pattern: many small synchronous requests => network latency amplification. two orthogonal areas to check: network path (hops, NAT/firewall queuing, MTU, window scaling) and serialization/CPU on the sidecar that does KV -> model IO.
[01:35] Evan Morales: can you explain streaming vs non-streaming impact? we enable streaming in some flows.
[01:41] Liam O'Connor: sure. streaming (token-by-token) keeps the model socket open and sends partial output as it's generated; it reduces end-to-end latency for early tokens, but it increases the number of small network writes and potentially more context switches if the service isn't optimized for continuous batching. non-streaming (buffer until complete) can batch tokens internally and amortize KV lookups, but increases first-byte latency. tail behaviour differs: streaming can see spikes if network gets jittery or Nagle algorithm interacts with small writes.
[02:17] Priya Singh: we also do TLS termination on a load balancer in front of the path—would mutual TLS help?
[02:24] Liam O'Connor: mTLS reduces handshake frequency if you can reuse connections; main thing is connection reuse and keepalives. short-lived connections + per-request TLS handshake will kill p99. also check cipher suites—some older cpu-heavy suites cost ms each handshake.
[02:41] Jared Holt: is there a Redwood-side K-V cache pattern that reduces serialization overhead? we saw the 'K-V cache' doc but not implementation details.
[02:50] Maya Chen: yes, two quick approaches: 1) batch KV fetches at the request layer and send a single serialized payload per request; 2) use a binary on-the-wire format with zero-copy deserialization (we use flatbuffers-like serialization for some customers). also sharded hotkey handling: if a small set of keys is hot, shard them across instances and use sticky routing to avoid cross-instance hops.
[03:21] Evan Morales: shard + sticky routing could be tricky with autoscaling. you have suggestions?
[03:26] Liam O'Connor: sticky routing plus consistent hashing with rebalancing windows. additionally, implement a small in-process LRU for absolute hot keys, that reduces network hops entirely. small memory tradeoff but big tail latency wins.
[03:44] Priya Singh: we do observe spikes when autoscale pods spin up and warm caches are cold. any warmup recommendations?
[03:51] Liam O'Connor: pre-warming using synthetic traffic that populates KV and prefix caches; or seed caches from snapshot on startup. also prefer gradual scale policies over instant multipod jumps.
[04:08] Jared Holt: what about quantization affecting CPU vs memory and thus latency? we plan to run 4-bit quantized weights on serving.
[04:15] Maya Chen: quantization reduces GPU mem & compute, but can introduce extra CPU post-processing for dequantize/pack. If your runtime moves dequantize on the host or has copy paths that block the main thread, that can add ms. Redwood's runtime offers quantize-optimized execution paths to keep dequantize on-GPU for common architectures—worth validating with a GPU microbench.
[04:44] Evan Morales: can we get a test harness?
[04:47] Maya Chen: yes we'll share a harness that includes: synthetic request generator, control over streaming vs buffered, KV miss/hit patterns, ability to inject artificial hop latency and MTU mismatch.
[04:59] Priya Singh: on the network side, we'll capture pcap and TCP stats. we can also test jumbo frames (MTU 9000) in our transit path but need to check firewall support.
[05:10] Liam O'Connor: also collect per-connection RTT percentiles, retransmits, and TCP SACKs—those explain sudden tailness. Application-layer retries without backoff can amplify spikes.
[05:28] Evan Morales: what about fallback model strategy? if p99 goes over threshold, route to smaller model?
[05:33] Maya Chen: yup—routing fallbacks to a cheaper/lighter model in a different availability zone reduces p99 at cost of some quality. Redwood supports policy-based routing (by latency or cost) and automatic fallback when timeout thresholds are hit. we discussed canary rollouts last week.
[05:50] Jared Holt: any suggestions for buffering vs streaming hybrid?
[05:54] Liam O'Connor: hybrid: stream first N tokens then buffer to form small batches for the rest. or use early partial responses for high-confidence tokens and buffer the rest. instrumentation is key: measure token latency distribution, not just request latency.
[06:12] Priya Singh: about KV serialization: we noticed CPU spikes on the sidecar when handling large blob values. could compress?
[06:18] Maya Chen: compression helps bandwidth but adds CPU before model op. If the bottleneck is network bandwidth (small MTU with many packets), compressing may win. If the bottleneck is single-threaded serialization CPU, move to multi-threaded deserialization or pre-serialize on writer side.
[06:38] Evan Morales: any quick wins we can do in next week?
[06:42] Liam O'Connor: yes: 1) enable connection pooling / keepalives to avoid per-request TLS handshake; 2) batch KV fetches (client side) to reduce number of wire ops; 3) add small in-process hotkey cache for absolute hotkeys; 4) run the Redwood harness with artificial hop to replicate p99 and share traces.
[07:03] Maya Chen: ok we'll also provide recommended kernel settings (tcp window, txqueuelen, and disable GSO/GRO where problematic) and a sample iperf/pcap recipe so your network team can reproduce.
[07:18] Priya Singh: about VPC peering—what about cross-account routing and source/dest checks? we've had issues with asymmetric routing.
[07:24] Liam O'Connor: asymmetric routing causes stalls: ensure symmetric path, BGP preferences, and NAT session affinity. Also prefer single aggregating NAT device with sufficient conntrack table size.
[07:38] Jared Holt: will you provide a checklist for the infra team?
[07:41] Maya Chen: yes, checklist + benchmark harness. we'll also include a minimal config for jumbo frames test and recommended cipher suites.
[07:52] Evan Morales: timeline? we want bench results early next week.
[07:55] Maya Chen: action items captured. we'll send harness today, you run and upload traces, we'll analyze and reconvene.
[08:05] Priya Singh: one quick callout—we use an edge WAF that can delay small payloads for inspection. could that be the cause?
[08:11] Liam O'Connor: WAFs can introduce variable latency on small packets—yes that's plausible. try bypassing for test or whitelist the service.
[08:30] Closing recap and next steps:
- Redwood to share micro-benchmark harness + network recipe (Maya)
- Redwood SE to run KV serialization profiler and outline serialization/flatbuffer options (Liam)
- Rift to provide ingress IPs, p95/p99 SLAs, and sample pcaps (Priya)
- Meet in follow-up ~2026-05-18 to review traces and proposed mitigations

End of meeting.
